## Simple explanation

Continuous integration (CI) is a practice where developers integrate
changes into a shared codebase regularly, and automated checks run to
detect problems early.

## Technical explanation

A CI pipeline is triggered by events such as a push or pull request. It
may install dependencies, run tests, check formatting and types, build
artifacts, and publish results. CI validates code changes; it is distinct
from continuous delivery or deployment, which automate release steps.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

AI applications combine software, data pipelines, prompts, model
configurations, and evaluation logic. Automated checks help detect
regressions and make changes more reproducible, though tests must be
designed to account for nondeterminism, data access, and model costs.

## How it works

The repository defines a workflow that runs in a controlled environment
when changes are proposed. Each job reports success or failure, and
teams can require passing checks before merging. Workflows should avoid
exposing secrets to untrusted code.

## Practical example

A pull request can trigger unit tests, static checks, dictionary-entry
validation, and a Quarto site build. The results help reviewers catch
broken links or malformed content before merging.

## Common misconceptions

- CI does not guarantee that software is bug-free.
- Continuous integration is not the same as continuous deployment.
- A passing test suite is only as useful as its test coverage and quality.
